headline: Convicted Frank founder Charlie Javice reportedly seeking Trump pardon, sources say
summary: Javice, serving over seven years for fabricating millions of customer accounts, is reportedly courting those close to the Trump administration for clemency.
details: Charlie Javice, the convicted founder of Frank, is reportedly seeking a presidential pardon, with her camp quietly contacting people close to the Trump administration. According to the WSJ, her name has not yet appeared on a formal clemency request list at the Justice Department.

This comes as the administration reportedly considers issuing around 250 pardons this summer to mark America’s 250th birthday. A wave of clemency requests is pouring in from white-collar defendants, including Sam Bankman-Fried.

Last September, Javice was found guilty of fabricating millions of customer accounts to inflate her startup’s value. She then sold Frank to JPMorgan for $175 million. She is currently serving more than seven years and is appealing her conviction, arguing the case against her was unfair.

JPMorgan may have additional reasons for concern given its past relationship with President Trump. In early 2021, the bank closed accounts tied to Trump and his businesses, a move Trump has since called political "debanking" and has sued JPMorgan and CEO Jamie Dimon for $5 billion.

Javice also has powerful allies, including Apollo’s Marc Rowan, an early Frank investor who testified on her behalf. Rowan has donated to Trump’s campaigns and has contributed millions more to Republican congressional groups since Trump's reelection.

headline: Windows 11 users frustrated by Microsoft account requirements creeping into OS features
summary: Windows 11 users are increasingly vocal about the mandatory Microsoft account integration, which is now extending to core operating system functionalities, causing widespread frustration.
details: Windows 11 users are expressing growing dissatisfaction with Microsoft's push for mandatory account integration. What began as a requirement for initial setup is now reportedly extending to more features within the operating system. This trend is leading to significant user frustration.

The increasing reliance on Microsoft accounts for basic OS functions is seen by many as an erosion of user control and privacy. Users report feeling locked into the Microsoft ecosystem, even for tasks that traditionally did not require online authentication.

Community discussions highlight concerns over data collection and the inability to fully utilize the OS without linking personal data to a cloud account. Many users prefer the option of a local account for enhanced privacy and simplicity, a choice that is becoming increasingly difficult to maintain.

The sentiment suggests a growing rift between Microsoft's strategy to integrate its services and user expectations for a more flexible and privacy-respecting operating system. This ongoing debate underscores the tension between convenience and user autonomy in modern computing.
